title: Notice of Amendment for Projects Located Off the Northeast Corridor for the Fiscal Year 2024 Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail Program
summary:
Two federal notices out today point in different directions: one speeds up border projects by waiving a wide set of environmental and cultural review laws, and the other fine-tunes a major rail grant process to avoid confusion and keep money moving to passenger rail projects.

The Department of Homeland Security issued a waiver so it can move faster on border infrastructure. It temporarily sets aside compliance with numerous environmental, historic preservation, and related laws for certain projects, keeps earlier waivers in place, and leaves the door open for more waivers if needed. Supporters will see this as a way to accelerate work they view as urgent for security and operations. Contractors and agencies involved in the projects may also benefit from shorter timelines. On the other hand, communities along the border, Tribal Nations, conservation groups, and historic preservation advocates may be negatively affected by reduced review and fewer protections, and they may have less opportunity to weigh in before work proceeds.

Separately, the Federal Railroad Administration corrected the listing for its current grant opportunity for intercity passenger rail projects outside the Northeast Corridor. The correct listing is on Grants.gov under FR–FSP–25–006, and applications are due by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 7, 2026. This cleanup helps states, rail authorities, and local partners find the right place to apply and keep projects on track. Applicants who rely on the earlier, incorrect listing could have been tripped up, and smaller teams with limited administrative capacity may feel the strain of the process and deadline. Still, the clarified notice should reduce confusion and help ensure eligible projects can compete for funding.

Taken together, these actions show the federal government pushing speed on border projects while tightening the paperwork on rail grants. Who benefits or loses will depend on your vantage point: quicker delivery versus thorough safeguards, and clearer grant guidance versus tight timelines.
